newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine wants money faster for Chernobyl close.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine wants money faster for Chernobyl close.

text.p: Ukraine's top Chernobyl negotiator said on Tuesday that Kiev wanted the West to speed up financing for closure of the notorious nuclear power plant.

Environment Minister Yuri Kostenko, speaking before a new round of talks with wealthy G7 nations, also repeated his call for removal of tonnes of nuclear fuel inside the ruined fourth reactor, which exploded a decade ago.
"Until now Ukraine has not gotten a single kopeck (from the West) to realise Chernobyl's closure," Kostenko told reporters.
"Even if we signed the first agreement soon with the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, then the first amount would only come in January of next year."
Kostenko said the EBRD is to allocate a grant of 118 million Ecu ($150 million) to "prepare the station for stoppage."

Further financing would be for construction of a special plant to reprocess radioactive materials, setting up a special nuclear research centre and completion of two new reactors at the Rivne and Khmelnitsky plants in western Ukraine.
Ukrainian and G7 nuclear experts are due to meet in Paris on October 10-11.
"We will put the question to them bluntly about starting financing for all these projects," Kostenko said. "Without money, these talks remain talks and promises remain promises."
But he added that Kiev itself was not quick enough in presenting concrete proposals.
"The West finances projects but not political intentions. Both grants and credits require concrete projects. Only then will the EBRD decide whether to go ahead (with financing)."
The G7 has pledged more than $3 billion in grants and credits for Ukraine's promise to close Chernobyl by 2000.
Kostenko said that Ukraine has given assurances that it will stop the first Chernobyl reactor next month and not restart it later.

Two working RBMK-type reactors, No. 1 and No. 3, at Chernobyl produce five percent of Ukraine's electricity. The fourth block exploded 10 years ago in the world's worst civil nuclear disaster. The block caught fire in 1991 and was switched off.

Kostenko said both Ukrainian and G7 experts had not yet decided whether to build a new sarcophagus over the ruined fourth reactor, begin dealing with the nuclear fuel inside it, or do both simultaneously.

Experts say there are between 90 and 200 tonnes of nuclear fuel inside the cracked sarcophagus. Last month metres measured a short-term increase of neutron higher activity within the structure, and some suggested it might be a small chain reaction.
"In general it would take dozens of billion dollars over 30 to 50 years to turn Chernobyl into an ecologically safe area," Kostenko said.
